name: Claude Certified Architect – Foundations
tagline: Make sound trade-off decisions when building production systems with Claude Code, the Agent SDK, the Claude API and MCP.
description:
The Foundations exam (code **CCAR-F**) checks that you can make informed decisions about trade-offs when you build real solutions with Claude. It covers **Claude Code, the Claude Agent SDK, the Claude API and the Model Context Protocol (MCP)**.

Every question sits inside a realistic production scenario. You get **4 scenarios picked at random from a bank of 6**: a customer support agent, code generation with Claude Code, a multi-agent research system, developer productivity tools, Claude Code in CI/CD, and structured data extraction. The exam tests judgment as well as facts. Often several options would work, and the right answer is the one that fixes the root cause with the least machinery.

The official guide aims it at solution architects with about 6+ months of hands-on work with the Claude API, Agent SDK, Claude Code and MCP. That experience is recommended, not required.

examInfo.format: 60 multiple-choice and multiple-response items (each item states how many responses to select). Scenario-based: 4 scenarios drawn at random from a bank of 6, delivered as blocks of about 15 questions each.
examInfo.delivery: Proctored by Pearson VUE: online proctored (OnVUE) or at a Pearson test center. Register through the Anthropic Partner Academy.
examInfo.cost: $125 USD per attempt (the fee at checkout reflects any partner-tier discount)
examInfo.prerequisites: None mandatory. Recommended: 6+ months of practical experience building with the Claude API, Agent SDK, Claude Code and MCP. Registration currently requires belonging to a Claude Partner Network organization and using a recognized company email domain.
examInfo.retakePolicy: Waiting periods grow with each failed attempt: 14 days after the 1st, 30 days after the 2nd, 90 days after the 3rd. Maximum 4 attempts per exam in a rolling 12 months. The fee applies to every attempt. You can cancel or reschedule up to 24 hours before the appointment.
examInfo.notes: Source: official Exam Guide v1.0 (effective July 2026, exam code CCAR-F), read in full. PDF: https://everpath-course-content.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com/instructor%2F6nizmqk8tpzpfjvt6qmmav7rh%2Fpublic%2F1783542750%2FClaude+Certified+Architect+%E2%80%93+Foundations+Exam+Guide.pdf. Scoring is criterion-referenced with a scaled cut score of 720. The score report shows percent-correct per domain, but only the total scaled score decides pass/fail. The credential is valid 12 months; on-time renewal is a free, non-proctored assessment on the Partner Academy. The guide says 'subject to change without notice', so re-check the Partner Academy before booking. Some candidate write-ups say validity is 6 months; the official guide says 12. The guide uses the name 'Task tool' for spawning subagents (current SDK docs call it 'Agent'); exam answers follow the guide's wording. Out of scope: fine-tuning, API auth/billing, deploying or hosting MCP servers, embeddings and vector DBs, computer use, vision, streaming/SSE, rate limits and pricing calculations, OAuth, cloud-provider configs, and prompt caching beyond knowing that it exists.

domains.name: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
domains.summary: The biggest domain, about 16 of 60 items. It covers running agentic loops on stop_reason, coordinator–subagent (hub-and-spoke) designs, passing context to isolated subagents, enforcing workflow order with hooks and prerequisite gates instead of prompts, choosing a decomposition strategy, and managing session resume and fork.

taskStatements.text: Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution
Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns
Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
Manage session state, resumption, and forking

domains.name: Tool Design & MCP Integration
domains.summary: About 11 items. It covers tool descriptions as the main way the model selects tools, structured MCP error responses (isError, error category, retryable flag), giving each agent a scoped tool set and setting tool_choice, MCP server scoping in .mcp.json and ~/.claude.json, and picking the right built-in tool (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob).

taskStatements.text: Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
Implement structured error responses for MCP tools
Distribute tools appropriately across agents and configure tool choice
Integrate MCP servers into Claude Code and agent workflows
Select and apply built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) effectively

domains.name: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
domains.summary: About 12 items, and the weakest domain for several candidates who passed. It covers the CLAUDE.md hierarchy and @imports, .claude/rules/ with path globs, project versus personal slash commands and skills (context: fork, allowed-tools, argument-hint), plan mode versus direct execution, iterative refinement, and running Claude Code in CI/CD with -p, --output-format json and --json-schema.

taskStatements.text: Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution
Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines

domains.name: Prompt Engineering & Structured Output
domains.summary: About 12 items. It covers explicit categorical criteria instead of vague instructions like 'be conservative', targeted few-shot examples, getting structured output through tool_use and JSON schemas (which fixes syntax but not meaning), nullable fields and enum 'other' patterns, validation-retry loops, choosing between the Message Batches API and synchronous calls, and independent multi-pass review.

taskStatements.text: Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives
Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality
Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
Implement validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality
Design efficient batch processing strategies
Design multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures

domains.name: Context Management & Reliability
domains.summary: About 9 items. It covers keeping exact facts safe from lossy summaries (a persistent case-facts block), the lost-in-the-middle effect, escalation triggers and clarifying questions, structured error propagation that tells access failures apart from empty results, scratchpads and subagents for large codebases, calibrated human review with stratified sampling, and keeping source provenance through synthesis.

taskStatements.text: Manage conversation context to preserve critical information across long interactions
Design effective escalation and ambiguity resolution patterns
Implement error propagation strategies across multi-agent systems
Manage context effectively in large codebase exploration
Design human review workflows and confidence calibration
Preserve information provenance and handle uncertainty in multi-source synthesis

scenarios.title: Customer Support Resolution Agent
scenarios.description:
You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.

Primary domains: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration, Tool Design & MCP Integration, Context Management & Reliability.

scenarios.title: Code Generation with Claude Code
scenarios.description:
You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.

Primary domains: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows, Context Management & Reliability.

scenarios.title: Multi-Agent Research System
scenarios.description:
You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

Primary domains: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration, Tool Design & MCP Integration, Context Management & Reliability.

scenarios.title: Developer Productivity with Claude
scenarios.description:
You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.

Primary domains: Tool Design & MCP Integration, Claude Code Configuration & Workflows, Agentic Architecture & Orchestration.

scenarios.title: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
scenarios.description:
You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.

Primary domains: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows, Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.

scenarios.title: Structured Data Extraction
scenarios.description:
You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.

Primary domains: Prompt Engineering & Structured Output, Context Management & Reliability.

name: Claude Certified Architect – Professional
tagline: Design, govern, evaluate and deliver production-grade Claude solutions, and defend each trade-off to stakeholders.
description:
The Professional exam (code **CCAR-P**) checks that you can design, build and deliver production-grade AI solutions on Anthropic's Claude platform. That means selecting models, architectures and API patterns; applying prompt and context engineering; integrating Claude into enterprise systems (including RAG, MCP and observability); and building evaluation, security, compliance and governance into the design.

It is broader than Foundations and centers on judgment. Candidates describe it as "less about API mechanics … much more about judgement". About a quarter of the exam (Governance 14% + Stakeholder Communication 14%) covers owning a system in production and explaining trade-offs in business terms.

The official guide aims it at mid- to senior-level solution architects, AI/ML engineers and tech leads with 3+ years in systems architecture and 6+ months running Claude or similar LLM systems in production. That experience is recommended, not required. Foundations is **not** a prerequisite.

examInfo.format: 63 multiple-choice and multiple-response items (each item states how many responses to select). The official guide publishes no scenario bank. Third-party sources describe the items as standalone trade-off questions, unlike the scenario blocks in Foundations.
examInfo.delivery: Proctored by Pearson VUE: online proctored (OnVUE) or at a Pearson test center. Register through the Anthropic Partner Academy.
examInfo.cost: $175 USD per attempt (the fee at checkout reflects any partner-tier discount)
examInfo.prerequisites: None mandatory. Foundations is not required. Recommended: a foundation in software engineering best practices, 3+ years in systems architecture or platform engineering, 6+ months hands-on with Claude or comparable LLM systems in production, and experience delivering end-to-end from discovery through operationalization. Registration currently requires belonging to a Claude Partner Network organization.
examInfo.retakePolicy: Waiting periods grow with each failed attempt: 14 days after the 1st, 30 days after the 2nd, 90 days after the 3rd. Maximum 4 attempts per exam in a rolling 12 months. The fee applies to every attempt. You can cancel or reschedule up to 24 hours before the appointment.
examInfo.notes: Source: official Exam Guide v1.0 (effective July 2026, exam code CCAR-P), read in full. PDF: https://everpath-course-content.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com/instructor%2F6nizmqk8tpzpfjvt6qmmav7rh%2Fpublic%2F1783542810%2FClaude+Certified+Architect+%E2%80%93+Professional+Exam+Guide.pdf. The domains, weights and objective wording are verbatim. The guide lists each domain's objectives as unnumbered bullets, so the task statement ids here (1.1, 1.2 …) were assigned in the guide's order for tracking and are not official numbering. The guide includes only 3 illustrative sample questions (least-privilege tool removal, prompt caching with a stable prefix first, diagnosing a stale RAG index) and names no scenario bank. 'Standalone items' comes from third-party sources. Some third-party pages say 60 questions; the official guide says 63. No official practice exam was found. The official guide gives no detailed knowledge/skills lists for RAG, compliance, ethics or stakeholder management, so lesson depth in those areas draws on Anthropic docs and engineering posts rather than exam-specific statements. Scoring is criterion-referenced (cut score 720, scaled 100–1,000). The credential is valid 12 months with free on-time renewal.

domains.name: Solution Design & Architecture
domains.summary: About 11 items. It covers turning business problems into Claude solutions, end-to-end architectures with feedback loops, choosing among a workflow, an agent and an augmented LLM, multi-agent orchestration and decomposition, and tying designs to business value pillars and performance SLAs.

taskStatements.text: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)

domains.name: Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering
domains.summary: About 8 items. It covers model selection trade-offs (capability, latency, cost, context window), system prompts, templates and guardrails, zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought techniques, managing context windows and tokens, and reuse through prompt caching, modular prompts and Skills.

taskStatements.text: Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)
Optimize context windows and manage token usage
Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)

domains.name: Integration
domains.summary: The biggest Professional domain, about 12 items. It covers removing capability bloat (least privilege), finding authentication and authorization gaps, accuracy–latency trade-offs, observability at scale, RAG chunking, indexing and retrieval strategy, choosing MCP, API/CLI or agent-to-agent integration, and progressive discovery versus loading everything into context up front.

taskStatements.text: Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies
Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy

domains.name: Evaluation, Testing & Optimization
domains.summary: About 10 items. It covers defining metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security), building eval datasets with mixed grading methods (code, LLM judge, human), A/B testing and iteration, diagnosing prompt failures, hallucinations and model mismatch (check retrieval first), optimizing cost against performance, and monitoring in production.

taskStatements.text: Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch)
Optimize token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs
Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools

domains.name: Governance, Safety & Risk Management
domains.summary: About 9 items. It covers layered guardrails and safety controls, LLM failure modes (hallucination, prompt injection, compounding errors), human-in-the-loop as a hard gate in the workflow rather than a rubber stamp, regulatory compliance (GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP) that follows where the data flows, and bias, fairness and transparency.

taskStatements.text: Implement guardrails and safety controls
Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies
Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)

domains.name: Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Management
domains.summary: About 9 items. It covers structured discovery and gathering requirements, explaining architectural decisions and trade-offs in business terms, aligning expectations (including SLAs and non-determinism), documentation and implementation guidance, and supporting the lifecycle from discovery through handoff, monitoring and iteration.

taskStatements.text: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)

domains.name: Developer Productivity & Operational Enablement
domains.summary: About 4 items. It covers configuring Claude Code and related tools for teams (shared CLAUDE.md, managed settings, permissions, plugins, MCP), improving developer workflows with AI-assisted tooling (hooks, skills, subagents, CI), and supporting debugging and operational issue resolution.

taskStatements.text: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
Support debugging and operational issue resolution

name: Claude Certified Associate – Foundations
tagline: Use Claude well at work: write clear prompts, check every output, pick the right feature and model, and know when to escalate.
description:
The Associate exam (code **CCAO-F**) checks that you can use Claude to get real business and productivity work done with little hand-holding. You need no coding or API experience. It is written for people in operations, marketing, project management, education, communications, consulting and general knowledge work.

The exam rewards judgment more than feature trivia. The biggest domain is **Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)**: spotting hallucinations, verifying claims before they reach a real audience, and deciding when a human must review. Governance and responsible use (15%) and workflow design (16%) come next. Together, those three make up over half the exam. Prompt writing itself is only 14%.

You also need working knowledge of Claude's everyday features, including Projects (instructions plus knowledge), Artifacts, Research, memory, connectors such as Google Drive and Gmail, and the Haiku / Sonnet / Opus trade-off. You should also know where your role stops. The guide says Associates hand complex or technical builds to Claude Developers and Architects.

examInfo.format: 60 multiple-choice and multiple-response items (each item states how many responses to select). The official guide names no scenario bank. Its sample items are short, self-contained workplace situations (verify a cited regulation, pick a model for high-volume drafts, handle personal data under policy).
examInfo.delivery: Proctored by Pearson VUE: online proctored or at a Pearson test center. Register through the Anthropic Partner Academy, then schedule with Pearson VUE.
examInfo.cost: $99 USD per attempt (the fee at checkout reflects any partner-tier discount)
examInfo.prerequisites: None mandatory, and no software-development or API experience is needed. Recommended: regular hands-on use of Claude at work, a grounding in structured problem-solving, workflow design and digital tools, and a practical understanding of AI limitations (hallucinations, context constraints, data sensitivity). Exams are offered through the Anthropic Partner Academy for Claude Partner Network members.
examInfo.retakePolicy: Waiting periods grow with each failed attempt: 14 days after the 1st, 30 days after the 2nd, 90 days after the 3rd. Maximum 4 attempts per exam in a rolling 12 months. The fee applies to every attempt. You can cancel or reschedule up to 24 hours before the appointment (changes inside 24 hours forfeit the fee).

The domain names, weights and objective wording are verbatim. The guide lists each domain's objectives as unnumbered bullets, so the task statement ids (1.1, 1.2 …) were assigned here in the guide's order and are not official numbering. The guide includes 3 illustrative sample questions and no scenario bank. Scoring is criterion-referenced (cut score 720, scaled 100–1,000). The score report shows percent-correct per domain, but only the total scaled score decides pass/fail. The credential is valid 12 months, and on-time renewal is a free, non-proctored assessment on the Partner Academy. The official Partner Academy prep path has 8 modules (about 6.5 hours) that mirror the 7 domains. The guide names Haiku, Sonnet and Opus as the model types to tell apart. Anthropic's current lineup also includes a higher tier (Claude Fable 5.1), which the guide does not mention. Gaps: the guide gives objectives only, with no knowledge/skills lists, and the only public candidate report is a secondary relay (967/1000, 'moderate difficulty', business judgment over feature trivia). Product details (plan limits, feature names) change often, so lessons cite the Claude Help Center. The guide says 'subject to change without notice'. Re-check the Partner Academy before booking.

domains.name: Prompting and Task Execution
domains.summary: About 8 of 60 items. It covers writing clear prompts for business and technical work (context, goal, audience, format, examples), breaking big requests into steps, improving a prompt over several rounds instead of starting over, and changing your approach for analysis, research, drafting or brainstorming.

taskStatements.text: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
Iterate prompts to improve output quality
Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)

domains.name: Output Evaluation and Validation
domains.summary: The biggest domain, about 13 items. It covers checking Claude's output for accuracy and completeness, spotting hallucinated details (citations, numbers, names), inconsistencies and bias, and verifying against authoritative sources. You decide when human review is required, adapt output for its audience, and pick the right format: an artifact, inline text, or structured data.

taskStatements.text: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
Apply fact-checking and validation techniques

domains.name: Product and Model Selection

It covers choosing the right Claude feature (chat, Projects, Research, Artifacts), telling Haiku, Sonnet and Opus apart, and matching the model to the task's cost, speed and quality needs. domains.name: Workflow Integration and Solution Design
domains.summary: About 10 items. It covers using Claude to analyze requirements and use cases, research and plan, and improve or redesign existing processes (augment the work rather than replace judgment). You also need to explain Claude's value and its limits honestly to stakeholders, and to recognize when a solution needs a Developer or Architect.

Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration

domains.name: Configuration and Knowledge Management
domains.summary: About 7 items. It covers setting up Claude Projects with good instructions and the right knowledge files, managing uploaded knowledge and connectors (for example Google Drive and Gmail), writing system-level instructions that hold across chats, and keeping instructions and sources current so answers don't drift out of date.

domains.name: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

It covers judging which uses are appropriate and which are not, handling sensitive and regulated data (redact or anonymize before you upload, and follow policy rather than workarounds), following your organization's AI policies, and weighing ethical effects such as bias, transparency, accountability and overreliance.

taskStatements.text: Identify appropriate and inappropriate use cases

domains.name: Troubleshooting and Optimization
domains.summary: About 6 items. It covers diagnosing why output is weak (missing context, vague instructions, stale knowledge, too long a conversation, wrong model or feature) and applying the smallest fix that works. You adjust based on feedback and results, and make repeated workflows faster and cheaper without losing quality.

name: Claude Certified Developer – Foundations
tagline: Build, integrate and ship Claude apps, agents and tools: API mechanics, model and cost trade-offs, context, security and MCP.
description:
The Developer exam (code **CCDV-F**) checks that you can build, integrate and ship production-grade applications, agents and workflows on Claude at a foundational level. It covers the Claude API and client SDKs, the Claude Agent SDK, Claude Code, prompt and context engineering, model selection and cost, security guardrails, custom tools and MCP servers.

The blueprint is lopsided. **Applications and Integration is 33.1%**, about a third of the exam, and much of it is general software engineering: REST, JSON, async, version control, SDLC, code review, refactoring, requirements and configuration. **Model Selection and Optimization (16.8%)** and **Agents and Workflows (14.7%)** come next. Claude Code (3.1%) and Evals/Debugging (2.6%) are each worth only one or two items. Candidates say the main theme is trade-offs: batch vs realtime, built-in tool vs custom tool vs Skill vs MCP, which model tier, and where a guardrail belongs.

The official guide aims it at engineers with 1–5 years of software experience and 6+ months hands-on with Claude or similar LLM systems, proficient in Python and/or TypeScript. That experience is recommended, not required.

examInfo.format: 53 multiple-choice and multiple-response items (each item states how many responses to select). The official guide names no scenario bank. Its sample items are short, self-contained engineering situations (overnight bulk job, prompt injection from a web page, reusable access to an internal REST API).
examInfo.delivery: Proctored by Pearson VUE: online proctored or at a Pearson test center. Register through the Anthropic Partner Academy, then schedule with Pearson VUE.
examInfo.cost: $125 USD per attempt (the fee at checkout reflects any partner-tier discount)
examInfo.prerequisites: None mandatory. Recommended: 1–5 years of software engineering, 6+ months hands-on with Claude or comparable LLM systems, proficiency in Python and/or TypeScript, fluency with REST APIs and CLI tools, and a working understanding of LLM fundamentals, agents, context management and MCP. Exams are offered through the Anthropic Partner Academy for Claude Partner Network members.

The fee applies to every attempt. You can cancel or reschedule up to 24 hours before the appointment (changes inside 24 hours forfeit the fee).

The domain names and weights are verbatim. Weights are given to one decimal place and sum to 100.0. Each domain is split into named skills with their own exam-share weights (25 skills in total). Each task statement below is 'Skill name (skill weight %): official skill description', verbatim. The skill ids (1.1, 1.2 …) were assigned here in the guide's order and are not official numbering. About 53 × weight items per domain: D2 ≈ 17–18, D5 ≈ 9, D1 ≈ 8, D6 ≈ 6, D8 ≈ 5–6, D7 ≈ 4, D3 ≈ 1–2, D4 ≈ 1–2. Most of the exam sits in 'Software Engineering Foundations' (7.4%), 'Claude Application Design' (8.6%), 'Claude API Mechanics' (6.8%) and 'Technical Fundamentals' (6.1%). The guide includes 3 illustrative sample questions (Batch API for an overnight job, untrusted web content and prompt injection, an MCP server for a reusable internal API) and no scenario bank. Scoring is criterion-referenced (cut score 720, scaled 100–1,000), with percent-correct per domain on the score report. The credential is valid 12 months, and on-time renewal is a free, non-proctored assessment. The official Partner Academy prep path has 5 courses (about 13 hours). Some third-party pages list the domains with rounded weights. Use the guide's one-decimal values. Re-check the Partner Academy before booking, since the guide is 'subject to change without notice'.

domains.name: Agents and Workflows
domains.summary: About 8 of 53 items. It covers when to use a fixed workflow and when to use an autonomous agent, supervisor/subagent hierarchies, and building agents with the Claude Agent SDK or your own loop. You need to know self-hosted vs Anthropic-hosted (Managed Agents) deployment, hooks for deterministic actions, common patterns (tool-use loop, subagents, memory, context management), and where third-party frameworks such as Strands, LangGraph and PydanticAI fit.

taskStatements.text: Agent Architecture (4.5%): Principles, patterns, and tradeoffs of agent and workflow architecture, including the decision criteria for using a workflow versus an agent, the structure of manager/supervisor hierarchies, and the role of subagents in improving task execution.

Agent Construction with Claude (5.3%): Methods, tools, and platforms for constructing Claude agents, including the Claude Agent SDK, custom agent loops and harnesses, managed agent deployment models (self-hosted vs. Anthropic-hosted), and hooks for deterministic actions.

Agent Patterns and Frameworks (4.9%): Common agent design patterns (tool-use loops, sub-agents, memory, context-window management) and agentic abstraction frameworks (e.g., Strands, LangGraph, PydanticAI) for building agents and workflows for multi-step tasks.

domains.name: Applications and Integration
domains.summary: The biggest domain, about 17–18 items and a third of the exam. Claude API mechanics cover messages, tools, streaming, vision, thinking, caching, Batches vs realtime, and access through Bedrock, Vertex AI and Foundry. Application design covers how instructions behave across Claude Code, Desktop, claude.ai, the API and the SDKs, plus schemas, session hygiene and plugins. Configuration covers CLAUDE.md, settings.json, model version pinning and prompt versioning. The domain also tests a lot of general engineering: requirements, the systems life cycle, REST/JSON/async, git, SDLC, code review and refactoring.

taskStatements.text: Understanding Requirements (3.4%): Functional and infrastructure requirements based on business requirements and solution architecture.
Systems Life Cycle (2.8%): Systems life cycle management concepts and frameworks used to develop, implement, operate, and maintain IT systems.

Claude API Mechanics (6.8%): Claude API behavior and mechanics, including messages, tools, streaming, vision, thinking, caching, invoking Claude through third-party vendors, Messages API data access patterns, batch API use, and tradeoffs between realtime and batch API selection.

Software Engineering Foundations (7.4%): Core software engineering principles and practices, including REST APIs, JSON, asynchronous programming, version control, SDLC integration, code review, and small- and large-scale refactoring.

Claude Application Design (8.6%): Design considerations for building Claude applications, including how Claude interprets instructions across interfaces (Claude Code, Desktop, claude.ai, API, SDKs), content boundaries, schema design, session hygiene, and plugin management.
Configuration Management (4.1%): Configuration management for Claude system components, including CLAUDE.md files, settings.json, model version pinning, prompt versioning, and plugin dependencies.

domains.name: Claude Code
domains.summary: About 1–2 items. It covers Claude Code's building blocks (rules, Skills, slash commands, subagents, agent memory), session management, headless mode with -p and streaming output for scripts and CI, auto mode, the CLAUDE.md hierarchy, /init to set up a repository, and settings.json scopes. The domain is small, but these topics come back under Configuration Management and Claude Application Design in Domain 2.

taskStatements.text: Claude Code Operation (3.1%): Claude Code core components (Rules, Skills, Commands, Agents, Agent Memory), features (session management, built-in and custom slash commands, headless mode, streaming mode, auto-mode), the CLAUDE.md hierarchy, repository initialization, and settings.json configuration.

domains.name: Eval, Testing, and Debugging
domains.summary: About 1–2 items. It covers identifying the type of error (HTTP 4xx client errors, 429 rate limits, 529 overloaded, 5xx server errors, stop_reason outcomes such as max_tokens or refusal), choosing a recovery strategy (fix the request, retry with backoff, fall back, or escalate), reading traces to find the failure mode, and working out whether a problem comes from your integration code or from the model's output.

taskStatements.text: Debugging and Error Handling (2.6%): Debugging and error handling techniques for Claude applications, including error type identification, recovery strategy selection, trace analysis to identify failure modes, and problem origin isolation between the integration layer and model output.

domains.name: Model Selection and Optimization
domains.summary: About 9 items. LLM fundamentals cover tokens, context windows, sampling, non-determinism and next-token prediction, plus thinking modes, effort levels, fast mode and zero-, one- and few-shot prompting. Technical fundamentals cover SDKs that wrap REST and websockets. You also choose between Opus, Sonnet and Haiku on quality, latency and cost, handle breaking changes between model releases, and keep cost down with token tracking, cost modeling and prompt caching.

taskStatements.text: LLM Fundamentals (5.2%): Basic understanding of LLMs (tokens, context windows, sampling, non-determinism, next-token generation), model options (fast mode, extended thinking, adaptive thinking, effort levels), and fundamental prompting techniques (zero-shot, single-shot, multi-shot).
Technical Fundamentals (6.1%): Foundational technical concepts supporting AI application development, including basic engineering practices (integrating with SDKs that wrap REST APIs, websockets).

Model Selection and Tradeoffs (2.7%): Claude model capabilities (Opus vs. Sonnet vs. Haiku use cases, adaptive thinking support), tradeoffs across quality/latency/cost parameters, and breaking behavior changes across model releases when selecting models for tasks.

Cost and Token Management (2.8%): Token budgeting and cost management techniques for Claude applications, including token usage tracking, cost modeling, and caching techniques (prompt caching, cache check-pointing) for cost optimization.

domains.name: Prompt and Context Engineering
domains.summary: About 6 items. Context engineering covers keeping the window lean (prune tool output, compact, isolate work in subagents) to prevent drift and bloat. Prompt engineering covers clear instructions, few-shot examples, what goes in the system prompt vs the user turn, output constraints, input sanitization and iterating on prompts. Output handling covers structured outputs, validation, defensive parsing and not trusting confident-sounding answers.

taskStatements.text: Context Engineering (3.8%): Context and memory management techniques for Claude applications, including context window management, prevention of context drift and bloat (tool output pruning, compaction), and context isolation through subagents or multi-step agentic workflows.

Prompt Engineering (4.6%): Prompt engineering principles and methods (instruction clarity, few-shot examples, system versus user placement, output constraints, prompt and instruction placement across components, iterative refinement, prompt adjustment, input sanitization) when writing and iterating on prompts for Claude.

Output Handling (2.6%): Established patterns and techniques for producing, validating, and consuming Claude output, including structured output patterns, response validation, defensive parsing, and skepticism toward confident output.

domains.name: Security and Safety
domains.summary: About 4 items. It covers prompt injection and jailbreak defense (treat retrieved content as untrusted, keep it apart from instructions, least privilege), PII handling and data-leak prevention, and layered guardrails. It also covers using hooks to block destructive actions deterministically, and managing secrets and API keys across environments (never in prompts or repos), with identity checks and access monitoring.

taskStatements.text: AI Application Security (3.2%): Data privacy and security best practices, including prompt injection awareness and mitigation, jailbreak defense, untrusted input handling, data leakage prevention, PII handling, and ensuring authentication, authorization, confidentiality, privacy, and integrity.

Guardrails and Safe Deployment (2.3%): Safe and responsible deployment practices (content policy, guardrail layering) and secure-by-design principles (privacy, identity and access management, least privilege).
Claude Hooks (1.0%): Leveraging hooks for guardrails and safety controls to prevent destructive actions within Claude applications.

Identity, Secrets, and Key Management (1.6%): Managing secrets, credentials, and API keys across Claude development and production environments, including identity validation and authentication, access approval and level verification, and authorized access monitoring.

domains.name: Tools and MCPs
domains.summary: About 5–6 items. It covers implementing tools (function schemas, descriptions that drive tool selection, errors returned to the model, client-side vs server-side tools, approval gates), and building MCP servers (tools, resources, prompts, stdio vs HTTP transport, deployment and integration). The most-tested skill is choosing between a built-in tool, a custom tool, a Skill or an MCP server for a given need.

taskStatements.text: Tool Implementation (4.4%): Tool implementation practices for Claude applications, including tool use and function calling, configuration for external system interaction, tool description writing, error handling, tool usage patterns (agentic harness dispatch, client-side vs. server-side tools, approval patterns), and tool set construction best practices.

MCP Server Development (2.1%): MCP server development practices, including server authoring, deployment, integration with Claude applications, MCP resources, tools, and prompts, and communication patterns (stdio, sockets, client vs. server).
Agentic Customization (4.1%): Tradeoffs among built-in Tools, custom Tools, Skills, and MCPs for selecting and applying the appropriate approach for a given use case.
